analysis.one_liner: Writes EPA's cross-state smog and soot rule into law with later compliance deadlines for power plants.
analysis.headline: A bipartisan Senate bill to lock in EPA's cross-state air pollution rule was referred to committee, never received a hearing or vote, and died when the 112th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: EPA had finalized a rule cutting sulfur dioxide and nitrogen oxide pollution that blows across state lines from coal-fired power plants into neighboring states. This bill would write that rule into federal law, making it much harder to kill in court or by a future administration, but it would also push the compliance deadlines back by about two years — to 2014 for most reductions and 2016 for the deeper sulfur dioxide cuts. The bill went to the Environment and Public Works Committee and never moved again.
analysis.who_benefits: People living downwind of coal-fired power plants in other states, who would get legally enforceable limits on the soot and smog pollution drifting their way — the rule cuts sulfur dioxide and nitrogen oxide emissions that cross state lines [S2]. The sponsor's own state, Tennessee, sits downwind of such plants. A statute is far more durable than an EPA rule, which courts can vacate and administrations can rewrite.

how_it_helps.text: Enacts EPA's final rule on interstate transport of fine particulate matter and ozone into law, rather than leaving it as a regulation that a court or a later administration could undo [S2].

Sets fixed statutory deadlines: the rule takes effect January 1, 2012 for first-phase sulfur dioxide and annual nitrogen oxide reductions, May 1, 2012 for ozone-season nitrogen oxide cuts, and January 1, 2015 for second-phase sulfur dioxide cuts, with annual compliance checks starting April 1, 2014 and April 1, 2016 [S2].
Keeps EPA able to update the standards over time, since the bill applies to any update by the EPA Administrator, not just the original rule [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Coal- and other fossil-fired power plants in upwind states, which would have to cut sulfur dioxide and nitrogen oxide emissions on a fixed statutory schedule, with costs likely passed partly to their electricity customers. They get more time than the original rule gave them, but they lose the ability to challenge or repeal the rule outright.

drawbacks.text: The delays matter for health: sulfur dioxide and nitrogen oxide reductions would not be fully required until April 2014 and April 2016, so pollution the rule was written to stop would continue during those years [S2].

The bill leaves the burden of the emission cuts on power plants in upwind states, and those compliance costs tend to show up in electricity bills for customers in those states — this is the cost an honest supporter of the rule has to acknowledge.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core trade is durability versus speed. Writing the rule into law would protect real public-health gains from legal and political attack, which is why the sponsor — whose state breathes other states' pollution — backed it despite his own party generally fighting the rule. The price is about two extra years of cross-state pollution and higher compliance costs for upwind utilities and their customers. On balance the bill gives ordinary people cleaner air at the expense of a slower timeline for the industry it regulates.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Environment and Public Works Committee on November 7, 2011, received no hearing, markup, or floor vote, and died when the 112th Congress ended on January 3, 2013.

narrative.text: Senator Lamar Alexander introduced the bill on November 7, 2011, joined by Senator Mark Pryor as its one cosponsor, a Republican and a Democrat from two downwind states [S1],[S4].
The Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Environment and Public Works the same day; that is the last action the bill ever received [S5].
The bill never came out of committee and never reached the Senate floor for a vote before the 112th Congress ended [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Upwind coal-fired power plants came out ahead: no legally fixed statutory deadline was imposed, and the cross-state rule remained only an EPA regulation, leaving it open to court challenge and political repeal rather than protected in law as this bill would have done. Downwind residents never got the statutory backstop.

for.name: Sen. Lamar Alexander
for.role: U.S. Senator from Tennessee; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to codify the cross-state air pollution rule with delayed compliance dates.

for.name: Sen. Mark Pryor
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, the only cosponsor it attracted.

against.name: Senate Environment and Public Works Committee
against.role: Committee the bill was referred to
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after referral — no hearing, no markup, no vote — for the remainder of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: The bill's sponsorship crossed party lines — a Tennessee Republican and an Arkansas Democrat — but no roll-call vote was ever taken, so the partisan shape of any floor fight is unknown.

industries.note: The bill would have locked emission cuts into law, ending the industry's ability to attack or repeal the rule, but gave plants roughly two extra years to comply. Its interests run partly with the delay and partly against a permanent legal obligation.
Mandated sulfur dioxide and nitrogen oxide cuts at coal plants reduce coal consumption, and the industry's interest in blocking such rules runs against the cleaner air downwind residents would get.
Compliance costs at power plants tend to flow into electricity rates, so these households would bear part of the cost — alongside the air-quality benefit they and downwind neighbors receive.
